source.title: Safety Training May Persist Through Helpfulness Optimization in LLM Agents

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses prior findings about chat-model safety erosion but explicitly studies a different construct: agentic safety on ToolEmu, not refusal or harmful-request compliance. Its own results do not test the listed claim versions, and it does not rely on those findings as a tool.
record.gate_note: The paper cites earlier work on harmful-request refusal and benign fine-tuning, but those cited results are not this study's results. Its own ToolEmu safety scores concern risks from agents' actions on tasks, not refusal rates for harmful user requests. It does not measure per-token KL, compliant-prefix or suffix bypasses, decoding changes, safety-localized parameters, or the cause of first-token shallowness. Rows below record its reported agentic safety-persistence results as related findings, not as evidence for a listed version.
record.test_reason: The study's own results are ToolEmu agentic safety scores: risky tool calls on mostly legitimate, underspecified requests, graded by LLM evaluators. This is a different construct from harmful-request compliance (V1/V2). It also has no per-token KL (V3), prefill, suffix or decoding attacks (V4), parameter localization (V5), cause of shallowness (V6), or token-depth deepening (V7). Prior chat-setting erosion results appear only as citations. Per the rules, the findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. One addition: the authors also report that all tested open-weight source models were unsafe out of the box on ToolEmu (a "bias for action"). They also report that no configuration found Pareto-improving safe-and-helpful strategies.
record.recipe_differences: Uses LoRA DPO on agent trajectories and ToolEmu agentic risk/helpfulness scores, including sequential safety and helpfulness training; it does not use the original studies' harmful-request chat fine-tuning or refusal measure.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports effects across different source models, β values (0.05 and 0.1), LoRA ranks (16 and 64), evaluators, and training sequences. It says β=0.05 has slightly larger post-training effects; results for rank 64 are broadly similar, with average safety persistence 0.80 at β=0.05 and 0.92 at β=0.1.

fits_no_version.finding: After safety DPO, later helpfulness DPO kept most agentic safety gains on ToolEmu. Average Persist(S) was 0.84 at both β values (rank 16), and 0.80 and 0.92 at rank 64. NeMo 12B at β=0.1 was lowest at 0.64.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In ToolEmu agentic risk settings, safety gains from preference training largely persist through subsequent helpfulness DPO.

fits_no_version.finding: Helpfulness-only DPO did not lower agentic safety below the source models; it often raised it slightly. Example: Llama 3.1 8B safety went from 1.44 to 1.75 (Table 7). All source models scored poorly on safety out of the box.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Off-the-shelf safety-trained open models show low agentic safety (a bias for action), and helpfulness DPO does not further erode it in ToolEmu.

record.problems: The authors note the limited scope: one benchmark, four source models, LoRA rather than full-rank DPO, and no mechanistic explanation. They also note that the helpfulness training setup could be globally ineffective, which they have not ruled out. Evaluations rely on LLM evaluators.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 7–9 and Figures 3, 7, and 9–12 report additional per-model scores, other training sequences, evaluator-specific results, and rank-64 results. These are not separately extracted because they concern the same different agentic-safety construct; the persistence values in Table 1 directly summarize the main related outcome.

untested.parts: Harmful fine-tuning examples and the resulting harmful-request compliance.
Benign fine-tuning and harmful-request compliance. Helpfulness DPO on agent trajectories is measured only against ToolEmu risky-action safety, not refusal of harmful requests.
Per-token KL by response position between aligned and base models.
Prefilling, adversarial suffixes or decoding changes.
Localization of safety in few weights or ranks. LoRA ranks 16 and 64 are training choices, not localization tests.
Data or training-objective causes of first-token shallowness.
Training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens, and its robustness.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly linked to none. Their states describe persistence of the related agentic finding, not any claim version. R9 (1.05) exceeds 1; the authors attribute values above 1 to noise. The persistence baseline is the helpfulness-only model, not the source model.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning examples and harmful-request compliance/refusal.
Ordinary or carefully chosen benign data and harmful-request compliance/refusal; helpfulness DPO on agent trajectories is not this measure.
Per-token KL by response position for aligned and base models.
Compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes and harmful completion rates.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries refusal behavior.
Whether data or training objectives cause first-token shallowness.
Training that spreads safety beyond initial response tokens and its robustness.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B
rows.operation_detail: Safety persistence after sequential LoRA DPO: safety training followed by helpfulness training

conditions.value: ToolEmu; averaged over 72 test tasks, two evaluators, and three seeds

rows.measure: Safety persistence metric (fraction of safety-training gains retained after helpfulness training)
rows.note: The metric compares safety training followed by helpfulness training against helpfulness-only and safety-only configurations. It measures agentic ToolEmu safety, not harmful-request refusal.
